newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian minister calms brokers as stocks plunge.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian minister calms brokers as stocks plunge.

text.p: Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad paid a surprise visit to the stock exchange on Thursday to bolster confidence as the market index suffered one of its sharpest one-day falls.

The composite index ended down 21.92 points, or 3.13 percent, at 677.94 points after being hit by accumulated concern over higher interest rates, new margin finance regulations and payments due on large rights issues.
"The tight rupiah policy on the fiscal and monetary side will be adjusted according to market conditions, that means it will be eased in steps," Mar'ie told reporters after the visit.
One broker said the minister's visit to the exchange had possibly prevented a steeper fall.
"The surprise visit has bolstered sentiment. The index may have closed much lower if the minister did not visit," he said.

The market recorded its second steepest intra-day fall on record when it dipped to 673.72 before pulling back up. The steepest plunge during the course of one day, 33.54 points, was on July 29 last year in the aftermath of the July 27 Jakarta riots.
"(The fall) is an accumulation of many things, with interest rates as the main reason," said Tom Ingles, head of research with ING Baring Securities Indonesia.

"We had expected it to fall because of higher interest rates, regulations on margin trading and rights issue payments," William Keeling, head of research with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Research in Jakarta, said.
Keeling added however that he had not expected the market to fall so steeply.

Bank Indonesia's recent policy of increasing short-term rates of central bank certificates (SBIs) and staying out of the short-term securities market (SBPUs) was aimed at reducing speculative attacks on the rupiah, analysts said.
The policy, however, had tightened rupiah liquidity, pushed up the rupiah interbank rate and prompted banks to increase interest rates, they said.
Keeling said some 6.74 trillion rupiah ($2.6 billion) in rights issue payments over the next four weeks was also one of the reasons behind the fall.

This is an unprecedented amount of fund-raising by existing companies and is equivalent to 2.6 percent of the Jakarta Stock Exchange's market capitalisation of 260 trillion rupiah. This excluded cash demands made by new IPOs, Keeling said.
Analysts and brokers said the new margin finance regulations which limit domestic retail client leverage were also seen triggering the panic selling.
"The introduction of margin finance regulations may, if immediately and strictly enforced, cause disruption," Keeling said.
A growing proportion of retail investors are operating on margin finance.

The typical margin investor is probably 300 percent geared on the underlying cash deposit held by the stockbroking company. If the client is fully invested and is faced by a rights issue, the only options are to increase leverage or sell stock, Keeling said. ($ = 2588 Rupiah)
